analysis.one_liner: Restores and expands disability benefits for coal miners with black lung and tightens rules on companies contesting their claims.
analysis.headline: Sen. Casey's bill to improve black lung benefits for coal miners drew five Democratic senators' support but never received a hearing or vote, dying in committee when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Coal miners who develop black lung disease from breathing coal dust are entitled to federal disability benefits, but claims often turn into years of adversarial litigation against the mine operator. This bill would have raised and inflation-indexed benefit payments, made it easier for severely ill miners and their survivors to qualify, paid miners' lawyers' fees out of the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund for stalled claims, required operators to share all medical evidence with claimants, imposed fraud penalties and lawyer disqualification, and set up an impartial panel to read chest x-rays instead of leaving readings to doctors hired by the companies. It also directed a study of whether coal dust limits should be tightened further. The Senate referred the bill to its Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never acted, and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners with black lung disease and their surviving spouses and dependents. The bill would have raised the benefit floor to $7,980 per year starting in 2015 with annual cost-of-living increases, created an automatic entitlement for miners with the most advanced disease, allowed miners who had their claims denied based on x-ray readings the Labor Department later deemed unreliable to refile within one year, and paid attorneys' fees and some medical-expense costs for qualifying contested claims out of the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, with operators reimbursing the fund when benefits are awarded.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal miners with black lung disease

how_it_helps.text: It raises disabled miners' annual benefit to $7,980 starting in 2015, replacing the tie to federal pay scales that had frozen their benefits during federal pay freezes, and indexes it to inflation each year after.

It creates an irrebuttable presumption of total disability for miners diagnosed with complicated pneumoconiosis or progressive massive fibrosis, the most advanced forms of the disease, and a rebuttable presumption for miners with 15 or more years in the mines whose x-rays are negative but who show disabling respiratory impairment.

It lets claimants whose earlier cases were denied on chest x-ray readings that the Labor Department later deemed not worthy of credit file a new claim within one year, adjudicated without those readings.

It requires mine operators to hand over the examining physician's report within 21 days and to share all medical evidence with the claimant even if they do not plan to use it, ending the practice of withholding evidence from miners and judges.

It establishes a NIOSH pilot program of independent three-physician panels to classify chest x-rays, with conflict-of-interest screening and a binding ethics code, in place of readings by company-retained doctors.

It makes it a crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, to make false statements in black lung proceedings or to threaten or mislead participants, and permanently disqualifies attorneys or expert witnesses who do so.

It directs the Labor Department to study whether respirable coal dust limits should be lowered, using data from continuous personal dust monitors, and to revise the standard if the evidence supports it.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, who would face greater benefit liability, a duty to share evidence, fraud and disqualification penalties, and reimbursement of the fund for fees and medical expenses when benefits are awarded; the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which pays these costs up front and is financed by excise taxes on coal. Operators could pass some of the higher benefit liability through, and the fund's deficits are ultimately a federal fiscal matter.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and the trust fund

drawbacks.text: The new benefit floor ($7,980 per year in 2015) and expanded presumptions increase charges against the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which operators reimburse only in claims where a liable operator can be identified and pays; claims traced to defunct operators stay on the fund, which is financed by a coal excise tax.

Higher benefit liability and a possible lower dust standard land on coal companies at a time when the industry was contracting, which operators argued threatened jobs in coal-dependent communities; the bill contains no transition aid for those regions.

The B Reader panel program, mandatory training, disclosure rules, and mandated reports add administrative machinery and cost to a claims system the bill itself acknowledges already averaged 40 months per decision before an administrative law judge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is strong on its own terms: the text documents operators' lawyers withholding medical evidence, company-retained physicians systematically misreading x-rays, and benefits that stopped rising with the cost of living. The benefits at stake are modest (a few hundred dollars a month for miners who can no longer breathe), and the cost falls largely on the companies whose dust exposure caused the disease. The honest costs are real but narrow: pressure on coal employment in already struggling regions and a trust fund whose liabilities grow when operators are insolvent. The bill was also heavy on process — reports, panels, training — which could slow rather than speed adjudication.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or vote, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Casey of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on September 29, 2015, joined by four Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Brown, Manchin, Warner, and Kaine.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral was the only action ever taken; the committee never reported the bill, and no vote was ever held in either chamber before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

The bill's findings describe the system it targeted: claims averaging 40 months before an administrative law judge, only 30 percent of claimants represented by a lawyer at the initial determination, evidence withheld by operators' legal representatives, and NIOSH-certified readers who misclassified x-rays while working for coal operators or their law firms.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators and the law firms and physicians they retain in black lung cases are better off because the bill died. None of its requirements took effect: operators keep the litigation practices the bill targeted — withholding medical evidence and relying on company-favorable x-ray readings — and no benefit increase, fee reimbursement, or dust-standard review was ever mandated.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey, Jr.
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its companion reforms to black lung claims processing.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; cosponsor

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Senate committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-TN) in the 114th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five senators behind the bill were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee that controlled its fate never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have raised their benefit liability, required them to hand over all medical evidence, subjected them and their lawyers to fraud penalties and disqualification, and required reimbursement of the fund for fees and medical costs when benefits are awarded. It also opened the door to a stricter coal dust limit, which directly raises their compliance costs. Their savings came from contesting claims successfully; the bill's premise was that those savings came partly from unfair process.

industries.industry: Physicians and law firms retained by coal operators in black lung cases
industries.note: The bill would have screened company-retained physicians out of claimant evaluations for two years, imposed conflict-of-interest disclosure and a binding ethics code, and permanently disqualified any expert or lawyer who made false statements. The bill's findings record that some NIOSH-certified readers systematically misclassified x-rays while working for operators or their firms, and that some operators' lawyers withheld evidence from miners and judges.

industries.industry: Black lung clinics and miners' attorneys
industries.note: Clinics would have gained explicit funding to help miners and families file claims, and attorneys would have had fees of up to $4,500 paid from the trust fund in contested claims that dragged past one year, removing the fee risk that leaves most claimants unrepresented (only 30 percent had a lawyer at the initial determination, per the bill's findings).
